en: The Sahaja Two-Armed Hevajra Sādhana of the venerable master Ācārya Śrīmad Alalavajrapāda.
Homage to the glorious Hevajra!
Having prostrated to one's own mind—which is all-giving, all-encompassing, the Guru, and Hevajra the Vajra-holder—I shall speak somewhat concerning the innate wheel of yoginīs. (1)
The mind is naturally pure, its essence being the nature of both the stable and the moving; it is stainless, devoid of subject and object, incomparable, unborn, non-dual, and like space. (2)
That very mind is the Sugatas, along with their Sons, the Wrathful Deities, and all the gods;
the mind and these three realms are equal—may the world be happy! (3)
The universe is not annihilated, for by its very nature it is like space; thus, though it is eternally non-adherent,
it possesses the property of being a mere illusion that accomplishes all purposes.
And it is perceived as having the nature of cognition. ||4||
The two parts of the beginning and the end have been uprooted from the very root through the disappearance of conceptual construction;
externally, there is no world-picture born again through the power of mental delusion.
Since it has been conquered by the elimination of obscuration and diminution, O wise ones, let this clarity be cultivated.
And for those possessing thorough knowledge, existence is declared by the Victors to be peace. ||5||
These forms and so forth that appear here, produced from a mind whose nature is peace,
are experienced as having the form of a deity.
They become bestowers of the fruit that is the glory of Buddhahood. ||6||
Enter into that state where existence becomes tranquility, one's own mind becomes the state of a Victor, and the multitude of afflictions becomes the factors of enlightenment.
In this path of the Omniscient One, which is exceedingly pure.
The mind bound by the latent impressions of ignorance is proclaimed as "bound"; that very same mind, when freed from those impressions, is designated as "liberated. (8)
The mind is free from bondage and liberation, devoid of delusion; for it is unconstructed and liberated from being existent, non-existent, both, or other than these. (9)

Through the connection with the habitual tendencies of one's own conceptual construction, that very mind of awakening (bodhicitta), which has emptiness and compassion as its essence, abides in the state of conventional reality. ||10||
It stands like a cow to lead [beings] from suffering through successive generations, and like a wish-fulfilling gem, it bestows the fruits of all desired objects. //11//
The Vajradhara taught that the mandala arises from the seed-syllables marked by the lotus, moon, fire, wind, water, and earth; however, for children, that is not according to reality.

The mandala of the glorious Hevajra, the wielder of the vajra, has arisen and is perfected, joined by the host of deities consisting of the completely purified aggregates, elements, and so forth. (13)
The perfected lotus-moon of the space-element is peaceful, of the nature of the unchanging, and liberated from unreal conceptualization by virtue of its being the essence of the Bhaga-gnosis. (14)
From that, the entire world arises according to the sequence of emanation;
from the inexpressible, it takes the form of the cause and becomes firmly established in the form of the fruit.
The world, consisting of the stable and the moving, is clearly manifested by shimmering rays of light;
it is an inconceivable and infinite creation, the abode of all the qualities of the Buddhas. (16)
Therefore, having fully worshipped that very [reality] through both external and internal worship, form, fragrance, touch, taste, and sound are experienced. (17)
All such things as these are declared to be external worship;
however, for the holders of the three vajras, thorough knowledge of reality as it is constitutes external worship. (18)
The confession of sins consists of acknowledging the mental action of the past as a loss;
it also includes engaging in virtuous dharmas and rejoicing in merits. (19)
The destruction of the reliance on false paths, and the purification of body, speech, and mind—this is considered the pure Three Refuges. (20)
The arising of the thought of awakening is a mind striving for the welfare of the world;
"all this is its very own mark"—thus it was taught by the Sage. (21)
Therefore, by its very nature, there exists toward sentient beings a love like that for a beloved son;
it is the desire to rescue both oneself and others from suffering, or from the cause of suffering. (22)
That compassion is also natural and remains unconditioned;
for that which arises as happiness through the attainment of happiness by others [is compassion]. (23)
The constant joy of one whose mind is free from desire is considered sympathetic joy (*muditā*);
it arises from contemplating the means to fulfill the vow to benefit the world. (24)
The relinquishing of other meanings is proclaimed as equanimity;
thus, the world is empty, devoid of intrinsic nature, and like the moon reflected in water. (25)
The world, born of cognition, is said to be devoid of the four alternatives;
it is empty by virtue of being without intrinsic nature, and its appearance is without cause. (26)

Through the departure of the upward [tendency], the entire world is devoid of aspiration; through the destruction of artificial conceptualization, it has the characteristic of being unconditioned. //27//
Therefore, the aggregates and so forth are empty because they are unarisen from the very beginning;
thus, through the nature of the coemergent, the awakening to emptiness is supreme. (28)
The great roar of perfect knowledge destroys the path of ignorance; mind-only is the imperishable, pure, and manifest reality established as arising from that. (29)
Adorned by walls in the form of the directions extending to the limits of infinite space, it stands upon a ground made of vajras in the midst of the sky-cage. (30)
Without beginning or end, peaceful, and pure, it is the maṇḍala of the three realms;
therein resides the unchanging one who holds the mind-vajra at its center. (31)
That very [state] is declared to be the Innate (sahaja); it is the second, the gathering of the seed-syllable (bījasaṅgraha).
Born from the seed-syllable of its own sign, it knows the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. 32.
The knower of reality himself has stated that the third [stage] is the "accomplishment of the image" (*bimba-niṣpatti*).
In that regard, it is the deity wherein the mind, by its very nature, remains in a state of peace. (33)
The seed-syllable is without support, the fourth state, the very placement of the imperishable;
it is born from emptiness and compassion, having the nature of the non-duality of wisdom and means. ||34||
The world-as-Hevajra with two arms abides in the form of the Innate;
likewise, in the eight directions of the eightfold circle, there are the Yoginīs whose forms are desire. (35)
Established in their minds through the intrinsic nature of the Noble Eightfold Path,
they are clearly manifest with a blazing, radiant light, entirely free from all attachments.
The ten directions are filled with light arising from the seed-syllable in his heart;
millions of suns appear as if they were mere fireflies. (37)
The infinite fields that are the abodes of the Victors, which tremble at his mere breath,
are measured by the dust particles of those very fields.
The streams bring about the attainment of glory. ||38||
Seeing this entire world as stable, manifest, perfected, and as clear as a reflection in a mirror—one who sees thus is called a mirror. (39)
And because of its single form, equality is considered the sameness of self and other;
it is called "thorough investigation" because of the observation of the true nature of the clearly manifest aspect. (40)
Acting in that manner toward the tasks of the world is called the "performance of duties.
That which is born as the innate form, through the exhaustion of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, is always known as the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*; thus it is remembered. (41)
In this way, whatever world one perceives is the very nature of the mind;
the entry of the Jñānasattva occurs through wisdom, because the world is non-different from wisdom. (42)
Through the sprinkling of the nectar of gnosis and perceiving the mind as one, one’s crown should be occupied by one's own lord; this is the sealing of gnosis with gnosis. 43.
The *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body) is considered the *dharma* because it maintains its own form;
the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body) is called the body that enjoys all desires. 44.
Because it emanates the world, this body is designated as "emanation";
because ignorance is exhausted, this body is known as "great bliss. (45)
Thus, this entire mandala-circle is stainless,
consisting of merit and wisdom, manifold, faultless, and pure by its very nature;
it is something utterly wondrous, filled with the essence of the inconceivable great bliss-festival of sentient beings.
Be free from doubt and enjoy this world without a sense of "mine," for it was created by you alone. 46.
The universe, which is non-dual consciousness in nature, devoid of cause, formless, and not established because it is subject to decay and birth, is brought by Śrī Herukī to its dissolution. 47.
Now, purification—the cleansing of the body and so forth—is being explained.
Indeed, for all things whatsoever, purified suchness is considered the purification. (48)
Therefore, the aggregates, sense-bases, faculties, and elements are pure by their very nature;
through the eight qualities of sovereignty, they become an eight-petalled lotus. (49)
Since it eternally surpasses the three worlds with its splendor, it is described as being situated above the sun by virtue of that purity. (50)
The supreme mind, having reached its vital breath through abiding in the *dharmadhātu*, remains in the form of the innate (*sahaja*), because the world is the innate nature. (51)
The world is consumed by impermanence; therefore, his body is covered in dust.
He is adorned with garlands of fifty letters and a garland of severed heads. (52)
Because he possesses the nature of the five Buddhas, he is endowed with the five mudrās;
because the world has the single form of gnosis, he abides in a state of uniformity. ||53||
Because he possesses the nature of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, he bears a form that is non-dual in aspect;
because he is indivisible, he holds a vajra in his right hand as a sign of his skill.
Because she is on the left, Prajñā, whose form is the sword as her limb, is held in the left hand;
the skull-cup is in the left because it protects (*kaṃ*) bliss (*sukha*), that is, it purifies it. (55)
Adorned with two arms because his nature consists of merit and wisdom, he possesses a dark blue body out of aversion toward conceptual construction and the afflictions. //56//
Enraged for the sake of abandoning ignorance, he has three eyes because he possesses the three bodies;
established in the two truths, he stands with two feet. ||57||
Standing in the dance posture of half-lotus, as if mocking the entire universe, the self-existent one has hair pointing upward because his form transcends the universe. (58)

Now, this vow (saṃvara), which is not in contradiction with the state of being co-emergent (sahaja) and is endowed with all the qualities of all Buddhas, is described as being distinct from every other limb [of the vows]. (59)
The mandala is the footprint; it is called a mandala because of its being rubbed [or adorned].
The thorough knowledge of all phenomena is the worship; it is the supreme worship of wisdom. (60)

The movement of the hands is the mudrā; meditation is the contemplation of the innate (sahaja); the performance of praise, song, and so forth is the ritual activity (kṛtya); and the renunciation of all mental constructs is the offering (bali). ||61||
The sacrificial fire-pit is the form of the *śruva* ladle; eating is said to be the *homa* offering.
Drinking the nectar of the water of wisdom is the *japa*; speaking is said to be the recitation. (62)
But because the mind is the state of being a refuge, it is proclaimed as "mantra";
its wandering for the sake of sentient beings is considered the teaching through speech. (63)

That which is called the hand is the action-seal (karmamudrā); the arms are known as the dharma-seal (dharmamudrā); the intrinsic nature is the commitment-seal (samayamudrā), while the unsurpassed is the great seal (mahāmudrā). //64//
The recitation of the breath, benevolence and the other [immeasurables], the ākṛti [posture], freedom from passion, and meditation on whatever is desired—these bring about stability of the mind. (65)
When the mind is fixed upon dream-cognition, upon blissful meditation, or upon viewing sleep with equanimity, it attains stability through the eyes and other senses; this is most certain. (66)
The universal vajra has the form of bliss and illuminates the meaning of the single reality;
mounted upon the chariot of coming and going, it is inconceivable through oral instruction.
By the illustrious Lalavajra, the summary of the fivefold sequence, which was concealed within the Yoginītantra, has been indicated here in brief. (68)

For the yogin whose form has become manifest through the application of an exceedingly intense [meditative absorption], the vajras of body, speech, and mind do not perform actions or conceptual constructions. (69)
Having perceived death, separation from loved ones, disease, and the terrible ripening of karma through old age,
people should always remain with a steady state of mind.
Cultivate the state of your own deity with diligent effort. ||70||
Always protect these five qualities: faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
[guard against] those known as ill-will, sensual desire, restlessness, and doubt.
And abandon both drowsiness and the five [hindrances]. ||71||
By the command of Nandipāda, this brief *Siddhasādhana* has been written;
therefore, may the noble Vajrayoginīs always grant me their forgiveness. (72)
By whatever merit has been accumulated here through my writing of this sādhana, may the entire world become the form of glorious Hevajra. ||73||
Thus, this entire mandala is the innate, inconceivable, and absolute, abiding from beginning to end like a city in the sky;
it is manifest as the form of the identity of existence and peace, yet devoid of intrinsic nature.
May it prevail for the sake of all prosperity for those who partake in worldly existence. ||74||
Thus ends the *Sahaja-dvibhuja-hevajra-sādhana*.
This is the work of the venerable master, the glorious Alalavajrapāda.
